title: #theatre #broadway #westend
transcript: It feels like we're in an era of franchise plays right now, as in non-musical plays that are within a big media franchise. And I've heard some people criticize it as a money grab trend, and I don't disagree with that, but in a couple different ways, I think it's the lesser of two evils. So obviously, right now on Broadway, we have Paranormal Activity, the Game of Thrones play just premiered in the UK. Obviously we've had Stranger Things, the first shadow, as well as the Hunger Games play. And I would say this trend was more or less kicked off by the nightly benefit gala for the J.K. R*wl*ng “Women's Fund.” Notably, all of these examples originated in the UK, where they actually have a long history of adapting major properties into plays, whereas in the US, we tend to focus on musical adaptations. This was a stage adaptation of the book series His Dark Materials, which played at the National Theatre in 2003. So this isn't a new thing. But I think what is happening now, at least more than before, is this thing of the franchise play that tells a new story within the world. The Stranger Things and game of Thrones stage plays are prequels. The JK Rowling Benefit Fund is a sequel. And Paranormal Activity is just a standalone story, though with some elements inspired by the original film. And like, not to knock any of the beautiful adaptations that have been done in London, like His Dark Materials or My Neighbor Totoro. But just speaking more broadly on the principle of the thing. I think that within the framework of hypercommercialized theater, if we are going to be relying on big franchise IP, then I would rather it be an original story that kind of adds to the canon, contribute something, rather than just copy pasting what was on screen or on the page. And the other reason I feel like it's kind of a lesser of two evils is a similar point with regards to musicalization. Again, if commercial theater is going to be relying so heavily on recognizable IP, I would rather they do it without adding unnecessary songs. Obviously, that's not always the case. There are plenty of franchise stage shows that lend themselves well to be musicalized, but more often it feels like they just add songs because there's a perception that that's what you're “supposed to do” when you bring a major property to the stage. So we end up with shows that actually do benefit from the format of live theater, live spectacle entertainment, but they're kind of ruined by songs that aren't necessary and usually not very good. Also, for what it's worth, I do think there's a lot of artistry and a lot of sort of boundary pushing stagecraft taking place to develop these spectacle shows, and I do respect that. Again, like I said, I would prefer that we weren't relying so heavily on recognizable IP. But I would rather have something like this than something like this.
